vocabulary.definition: The written record of Divine Revelation found in the books of the Old and New Testaments.
The living transmission of the Church's Gospel message found in the Church's teaching, life, and worship.
The fallen state of human nature into which all generations of people are born, originating from the disobedience of Adam and Eve.
The heritage of faith contained in Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, handed down in the Church.
The first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy).
The power of the mind to think, understand, and form judgments by a process of logic, used to know God's existence.
The official list of inspired books of the Bible.
The way God communicates knowledge of himself to humankind, realized most fully in Jesus Christ.
Meaning 'Good News', referring to the four accounts of Jesus' life, teaching, death, and resurrection.
The denial of the existence of God.
The belief in one all-powerful God.
The belief in many gods.
The belief that God created the universe but takes no further interest in it.
The central mystery of the Christian faith; there are Three Divine Persons in one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Christ's work of redemption through His Passion, death, Resurrection, and Ascension.
Spiritual beings with intelligence and free will who act as messengers for God.
The official teaching authority of the Church, bestowed by the Lord on Peter and the Apostles and their successors.
The guidance of the Holy Spirit that enabled the human authors to record faithfully, and without error, what God wanted revealed.
The doctrine that the Bible is free from error regarding the truth God wishes to reveal for the sake of salvation.
The code of conduct given by God to the Chosen People, summarized in the Ten Commandments.
An Aramaic term of endearment meaning 'Daddy', used by Jesus to address God the Father.
Title for God regarding His role as the source of all existence.
An attribute of God meaning He is beyond full understanding or description.
The attribute of God that he is everywhere, unlimited, and all-present.
The attribute of God that he is all-powerful.
The attribute of God that he is all-knowing.
The gift given by the Holy Spirit to the Pope and bishops in union with him to teach on matters of faith and morals without error.
The Second Coming of Christ when the Lord will judge the living and the dead.
Stories or myths about the origins of the earth, humans, other creatures, languages, and cultures.
The 'fathers of the faith', male rulers, elders, or leaders (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob).
People sent by God to encourage the Chosen People and speak on His behalf.
The forty-six books that make up the first part of the Bible and record salvation history before the coming of the Savior.
The twenty-seven books of the Bible written in apostolic times, which have the life and teaching of Jesus and the beginnings of the Church as their central theme.
A statement of belief; sometimes a collection of creedal statements.
Hebrew word for 'Anointed One'.
An appearance or manifestation of God to humans (e.g., the burning bush).
The day when the Holy Spirit descended on the Apostles and gave them the power to preach with conviction the message that Jesus is risen.
The state of purification that takes place after death for those who need to be made clean and holy before meeting the all-holy God in Heaven.
The dogma that God's eternal Son assumed a human nature and became man in Jesus Christ to save us from our sins.
A Greek title for Mary meaning 'God bearer'.
Hebrew word meaning 'wind' or 'breath', often used in the Old Testament to refer to God's mysterious and powerful life-giving presence (Holy Spirit).
The story of God's saving action in human history.
God's gift of friendship and life that enables us to share his life and love.
A worldwide, official assembly of the bishops under the direction of the Pope.
The twelve men Jesus chose to help him in his earthly ministry; the term means 'one who is sent'.
The movement, inspired and led by the Holy Spirit, that seeks the union of all Christian religions.
The power, rooted in reason and will, to perform deliberate actions on one's own responsibility.
A follower of Jesus; the word means 'learner'.
A solemn agreement between human beings or between God and a human being in which mutual commitments are made.
The theological virtue by which one believes in all that God has said and revealed.
A practical judgment of reason that helps a person decide the goodness or sinfulness of an action or attitude.
Church Father who translated the Bible into Latin (The Vulgate).
Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church who authored the 5 Proofs of God's Existence.
The mother of St. Augustine, known for her persistent prayer for his conversion.
The first Native American saint, known as the 'Lily of the Mohawks'.
English anchoress and mystic known for her 'Revelations of Divine Love'.

timeline.event: Approximate time of Moses and the Exodus
St. Paul writes his Epistles (Earliest New Testament writings)
Martyrdom of St. Peter and St. Paul in Rome (under Nero)
Destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem
Gospels of Matthew and Luke written (approximate)
Death of the last Apostle (End of Public Revelation)
Birth of St. Augustine in Thagaste
St. Augustine becomes Bishop of Hippo
Birth of St. Francis of Assisi
Birth of Blessed Julian of Norwich

locations.name: Thagaste
locations.significance: The birthplace of St. Augustine (located in modern-day Algeria).

locations.name: Hippo
locations.significance: The city in North Africa where St. Augustine served as Bishop.

locations.name: Bethlehem
locations.significance: The city of David where Jesus was born.

locations.name: Rome
locations.significance: The center of the early Church where St. Peter and St. Paul were martyred.

locations.name: Jerusalem
locations.significance: The holy city where Jesus' Passion, Death, and Resurrection occurred, and where the Church was born at Pentecost.

trueFalse.statement: The word 'Trinity' appears directly in the Bible.
trueFalse.correction: The word 'Trinity' does not appear in the Bible, though the reality of the three persons is revealed in scripture.

trueFalse.statement: There are events in scripture where all three persons of the Trinity are present.
trueFalse.correction: Yes, specifically at the Transfiguration and the Baptism of Jesus.

trueFalse.statement: St. Paul wrote one of the four Gospels.
trueFalse.correction: St. Paul wrote Epistles (Letters), not Gospels. The Gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

trueFalse.statement: Matthew's genealogy links Jesus all the way back to Abraham.
trueFalse.correction: Matthew emphasizes Jesus' Jewish heritage by tracing him to Abraham.

trueFalse.statement: Luke's genealogy links Jesus all the way back to Adam.
trueFalse.correction: Luke emphasizes Jesus as the universal savior of all mankind by tracing him to Adam.

trueFalse.statement: Salvation is available even to those who don't believe in or follow Jesus Christ.
trueFalse.correction: The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ but seek God with a sincere heart may achieve eternal salvation.

trueFalse.statement: Jesus performed miracles such as nature miracles, physical healings, exorcisms, and raisings from the dead.
trueFalse.correction: Jesus performed all these types of miracles to demonstrate the coming of God's Kingdom.

trueFalse.statement: The Apostles started writing Gospels immediately after Jesus ascended to Heaven.
trueFalse.correction: It took several decades (approx. 30-40 years) before the Gospels were written; they first relied on oral tradition.
Mary is the first disciple because she was the first to say 'Yes' to God at the Annunciation.

trueFalse.statement: St. Augustine wrote the 5 proofs of God's existence.
trueFalse.correction: St. Thomas Aquinas wrote the 5 proofs of God's existence.
